thread.title_full: Nation's largest corporate landlord hit with 114 civil rights complaints over housing voucher denials - NewsBreak

author: Kim LaCapria
title: Nation's largest corporate landlord hit with 114 civil rights complaints over housing voucher denials - NewsBreak
text:
By Kim LaCapria ,
1 days ago Photo Credit: iStock Greystar, the largest corporate landlord and apartment manager in the United States, is facing a sweeping fair housing challenge after a watchdog group alleged that Section 8 voucher holders were turned away from company-owned apartment properties.
The scope of the allegations is one of the things that stands out.
Invisible People cited complaints that involve 114 properties, describing Greystar as the nation's largest corporate landlord and apartment manager.
Here's what to know The Housing Rights Initiative and the national law firm Cohen Milstein submitted complaints on July 14 in California, Maryland, Hawai'i, Michigan, New Jersey, Virginia, and Washington, D.C.
The filings accuse Greystar of 114 violations of state and D.C. fair housing laws.
Housing Rights Initiative said the claims grew out of undercover stings that began in October 2025.
Testers posing as prospective renters called 114 different Greystar apartments and, according to the group, encountered the same result every time: either Section 8 vouchers were rejected outright, or their use came with unlawful conditions.
The group said one alleged practice was refusing to include voucher assistance when evaluating whether applicants met income requirements.
Where landlords are required by law to accept vouchers, that approach can effectively prevent renters from qualifying.
Because Greystar has such a large national presence, the complaints reach beyond a small set of buildings.
The company operates more than 1 million apartments across the U.S., including about 235,000 in the states and district where the complaints were filed.
More background When renters rely on housing vouchers, an illegal denial can mean losing access to neighborhoods with better jobs, schools, transit, and stability.
It can also mean spending more time searching for housing , paying more in application fees, and facing a greater risk of housing insecurity.
The complaints also underscored a broader imbalance in rental housing.
Large property owners can shape what daily life looks like for tenants, influencing everything from where they live to which choices they can make inside and around their homes.
Landlords across the country have also been criticized for preventing renters from adopting money-saving lifestyle changes, including gardening and hanging clotheslines to dry their laundry .
Claims that a landlord this large may have disregarded voucher protections also deepen concerns that growing corporate control of housing will intensify the crisis rather than ease it.
What's being done? In addition to filing complaints, Housing Rights Initiative also published recordings from calls to Greystar apartments, building a documented record one conversation at a time.
In housing discrimination cases, especially when a company operates at this scale, that kind of evidence can be especially valuable.
Saving listings, emails, screening criteria, and notes from phone calls may help if something feels off. Fair housing groups, legal aid organizations, and local housing agencies may be able to help determine whether a denial crossed a legal line.
For tenants trying to change restrictive property rules more broadly — whether around outdoor drying, gardening, or other cost-saving practices — it can help to organize with neighbors and read up on how to change bylaws when working with landlords or community associations.
"Greystar has been committing mass civil rights violations at a scale unlike anything our organization has ever seen," said Aaron Carr, Founder and Executive Director of Housing Rights Initiative, per Invisible People.
"The largest landlord in America is the most discriminatory landlord in America."
